In the light of this background, how should we move to improve our procedures? Really, there are only two areas of disagreement. The committee has worked long and hard. It has made good use of the precedents and practices in other parliaments. It has presented a report to this house, which report we are debating today. Most of the recommendations are acceptable, but there are two areas of controversy, namely the additional responsibilities being given to standing committees, and the programming of legislation in the house.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
Dealing firstly with the question of standing committees, it seems to me that hon. members opposite are missing the point. They are complaining, for example, that by referring the estimates of the departments to the standing committees the government is attempting to take away from this chamber the responsibility and power it now has in the spending of the nation's money. What is really so startling about this claim is that they miss entirely the relocation of time that is involved, this new relationship between the studying of the estimates and their timing.
As it is now, I am sure all hon. members will agree that whatever study of the estimates is done in this chamber-and, as has been said before, there is a tendency to make speeches here rather than to study estimates-this study is always done ex post facto. The money is not only budgeted for but in most cases the estimates are considered in this house long after the fact.
An important thing to consider in referring these estimates to the standing committees under the proposed rules changes is that members not only have an opportunity in the committees to get a close observation and examination of the estimates, but they can do this at a time when it is meaningful. This is the point that seems to be entirely missed by hon. members opposite.
Neither can I understand their complaint that there is any loss of the power of this chamber. Under the proposed amendments to the rules the opposition is given an allotted number of days, any of which it can, upon the return of these estimates from the standing committees, set aside to examine the estimates in this chamber if it so desires. One must also point out that those 25 allotted days, plus three reserved for the examination of the final supplementary estimates-making


28 days in all-can be augmented further by the use of any of the eight days that are allotted to the throne speech debate, or any of the six days that are allotted to the budget- making in all a further 14 days-that are not used up for those purposes.
On all of these days the opposition can completely control the subject matter of debate in this house. So there is no substantial diminution of the days they are allotted under the supply procedure at the present time. Therefore the opposition loses no power or opportunity to insist that this chamber examine estimates in detail. Moreover, when the estimates are considered in the chamber, they will first have been attacked in a standing committee.
So it will be seen, Mr. Speaker, that the opportunity of the opposition to examine estimates in detail in the standing committees is provided, plus the opportunity, if they so desire, to bring the estimates back to the house in order to focus the attention of the chamber upon them. Now, then, can the opposition complain that this chamber is being deprived of the power that it should possess in respect to the expenditures of the nation?
The most interesting area of all has become that of programming. It seems to me that there are certain basic points involved here. In the first place, it is obvious to me as a new member that reforms of this sort toward programming are necessary. I do not have to turn to the traditions of parliament, or to the examples of other legislative assemblies throughout the world, to support that statement. I go no further back than September and October of this year, when we sat around here for three weeks listening to a small number of opposition members speaking time and time again on the same subject of farm legislation. I understand from actual count that one opposition member spoke no less than 12 times in a repetitive fashion on that very subject. Not only did these members individually repeat their own remarks and suggestions to the government every time they spoke, but one member after the other stood in his place to repeat what others had said. Surely, Mr. Speaker, it cannot be suggested, even taking into account my unpractised eye, that quality of debate improves in proportion to its length.
I was astounded to hear the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) actually make reference to the length of the flag debate in supporting his proposition that debate in this house should be unbridled, because, as we all

know, that is a far, far cry from the position that he took during the currency of that very debate. As a new member I am not afraid to say that the length of time spent in this house on the farm legislation was absolutely disproportionate to its importance; to its importance, that is, in relation to other matters of legislation that are waiting to get the attention of this chamber.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it is necessary that our procedures change. Not only is it necessary, but apparently in the minds of opposition members it is highly desirable. Certainly the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) stood on his feet to say that he has been a proponent of this programming idea for years, and in fact has called it "calendarizing" the parliamentary year.
Although it is necessary and desirable to change, the point that seems to be missed is that it is the responsibility of the government to take this step. If there is any doubt about this, then would hon. members opposite answer me this: When they go home for the Christmas vacation and are asked, by chance, why this house did not get around to considering, for example, the drug bill, is it possible that they might say to some of their constituents: "Well, you must understand that it is the opposition benches that control length of debate, so it is really not fair to blame the government for its lack of programming in bringing that legislation forward, because we in the opposition prolonged the debate on the farm legislation to the extent that the government did not have the chance"? If they do so, then I accede to their view that responsibility should rest on that side of the house in the matter of controlling time. But it is a false premise to believe that supporters of the opposition will be as generous as I have suggested. What they will do is blame the government for not knowing how to program their legislation. They will claim the government is disorganized and cannot bring forward important legislation; that the government does not know how to plan its affairs.
The government is visited with this awesome responsibility. If it does not take the action suggested in this report, there may not be a parliament left when next we seek to elect a new government. This government is considered by all Canadian voters to have the responsibility of taking this step, and the government is taking this perfectly correct step in moving directly and vigorously, and in a meaningful way, into the area of programming.

Too often we have seen reforms that are obsolete by the time they are introduced. Too often have we seen changes that are away behind the fact and the need. These proposals, as I see them, are not. They constitute a very meaningful and direct step, what I consider to be a courageous step taken by the government, one that I have absolutely no hesitation in transmitting to my constituents as an intention to stop pussy-footing around with the question of programming, and to deal with it in a logical and sensible way.
Given those facts, if you will, what, then, are the true logistics? Let us stop reducing this thing to ridicule, to one of one-man meetings. What are the logistics of setting up a programming committee? The very first consideration that comes to my mind is that in setting up a programming committee the government immediately sacrifices its majority position in the house, if its meetings are to be attended only by the house leaders. If there is anything more fundamental to our parliamentary system than that the government should enjoy a majority in the house at every point in its deliberations, then I do not know what it is. If the government sets up a business committee, which all members agree is a good idea, it will have only 25 per cent of the representation on that committee.

When one moves on from there to examine what must be done in the light of that consideration to resolve the difficulty that arises when that committee cannot agree or come to a unanimous decision, he must bear this representation factor in mind. It has taken a position as one member of a committee of four, and consequently surrendered itself. In any event, in any committee such as this you will ultimately bump up against the government's majority. Of course you do;

Motion for Concurrence in Report there is no way around it. I challenge any hon. members of the house to set up some committee like that to program the time of the house that does not ultimately bump up against the government majority. That is fundamental to the operation of this house. The choice is between continuing with the present chaos and getting into the question of programming, and leaving the resolution of disagreement in the committee, by making the committee bigger with a majority of government members, will not be more palatable to hon. members of the opposition.
It has been suggested ad nauseam that the good will of hon. members will resolve this crisis, and about that I want to make several observations. It has been said that the government does not need these residual powers, because the great likelihood is that in a very high percentage of cases the house leaders will agree among themselves. That may be the case. Certainly if the committee had been operating when the farm legislation was before the house, if the new rules had been operating, no matter whether some backbenchers liked the idea or not, that legislation would have been concluded by quick agreement on a much earlier date than it did. However let us examine the proposition that the government does not need this residual power, because the deliberations of the committee very likely will conclude on the basis of agreement. After all, we are only trying to allot time for the debating of subject matters we are all interested in, as citizens of the country. Either that proposition is true or it is not. If it is not, the argument is self-defeating; if it is true, then the government has that residual power to solve any disagreement. That residual power is so minor and will be so rarely exercised that I do not see why we need worry about it.
The second point about the good will argument is that it is said that the discussions and deliberations of this committee will be destroyed, so to speak, if the government holds a stick over its meetings and has the ultimate power. The suggestion is that if everything is left on the basis of consent, agreement and good will, everyone will go to the committee and discuss. I submit that a much more reasonable proposition is that unless the government holds the residual power to resolve any crisis, unless it holds the residual power which will avoid a boycott-and that has happened in fairly recent memory-then the deliberations of the committee will not be meaningful. If the government does not hold that residual power it will in fact get itself


into a situation where the tail will wag the dog. Finally, the one thing that seems to be absent from all opposition suggestions on the subject of good will is that good will does reside on the government side of the house.

I have attempted to say some of the things I felt it my duty to say and to examine some of the things that need examining. They say there is a generation gap in this country. I say that it is not with hon. members who are my contemporaries and of my generation that the difficulty lies. If one goes back in time a short distance only, he will see that many young people are coming forward; they are only five or ten years behind us. When one talks to them about this institution and about institutions in this country in general he does not find great respect for those institutions. I came to this chamber because I believe this parliament has to survive; it therefore must improve and expedite its procedures to get on with the business of the nation. If I had not believed that I would not be here, and I am sure that many hon. members of this house have come here because they have concluded that reforms must be undertaken. But, Mr. Speaker, they must be undertaken in a meaningful way.
I have concluded that parliament is dedicated to discussion, yes. But parliament is not an insular ivory tower, a private club where members sit around as in a debating society and discuss things at the expense of the needs of this nation. This parliament serves not only its members; it serves the people. If it fails to serve the needs of this nation it will disappear, because there are other forms of government that can replace it. I say therefore that this government and this parliament have a responsibility to introduce legislative programs adequate to meet the needs of the nation. The government has the right to expect that program to be considered. The opposition has the right to examine and criticize that program and expose its faults to the nation; it has the right to amend it where possible and, in any case, to vote for or against it as it sees fit.
May I conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying that in my humble opinion these reforms are only a beginning. They are not drastic; these are not terminal changes. These are beginnings, because there are other areas of major significance that will have to be changed. Certain parts of our procedure are difficult for new members to understand. For instance, it is difficult to understand why certain matters have to be talked out on a daily basis. Some things this nation will not tolerate any longer, and there are more reforms that will have to be brought up. I am therefore very encouraged that the establishment of a standing committee has been suggested.

I asked that it be discussed at ten o'clock, to find out whether Canada intended to ask this company to make parts for jet planes in this country, in order to provide jobs for Canadians and participate in regional development program so as to abolish regional disparities.
Mr. Speaker, Air Canada has ordered ten L-1011 jets which are to be manufactured by the Lockheed Company at a cost, apparently, of $175 million. The first six jets are to be delivered in 1972; three more will be ready by 1973 and the last one in 1976.
Air Canada has already ordered these 270-passenger planes, after spending nine months appraising the advantages of these aircraft and other similar models.
This giant aircraft, Mr. Speaker-for the information of hon. members who are not familiar with the statistics-has a cruising speed of 565 miles per hour, which is 15 miles faster than the DC-8 and DC-9 aircraft now used by Air Canada. The engines are made by Rolls-Royce and have a thrust of 40,600 pounds; they are therefore twice as powerful as the most powerful engine of the DC-8. Those planes will be used exclusively for domestic flights in North America.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, with regard to the contract given by Air Canada, Canadians, naturally- and here I speak for them before parliament -hope to be able to participate actively and intensely in the manufacturing of at least part of those aircraft, for instance, certain parts, as I suggested.
It may be an excellent thing to grant contracts to competent companies which are known for doing a good job but, to my mind, we must nor forget also that Canadians need employment, that they face huge and complex economic problems. In this regard, we do not know what to think because no statement has been made since the news of the contract came out. All Canadians are waiting to find out whether they can find there a source of employment.
This then was the purpose of my remarks this evening. I should like to get a reply to this question: With a view to encouraging decentralizing programs, with which it dins our ears every week, will the government sign agreements with the Lockheed company to give work to Canadians?
Mr. Speaker, I would like the spokesman for the Department of Transport to tell us-


I repeat to make myself clear-whether negotiations are now under way between the government, through Air Canada, and the Lockheed company, to arrange for the manufacture of at least certains parts in Canada to encourage and support Canadian labour.
Moreover, as I said before, the engines in these aircraft being Rolls-Royce engines, and as this English firms has a subsidiary in Canada, it therefore does not seem impossible that this new contract could give work to a good number of Canadians without interfering with the contract, since a number of those aircraft are already made in Canada; this is not something to be scorned in these days of unemployment, insecurity and regional disparity.
Mr. Speaker, I feel my proposal is quite acceptable. It surely calls for a positive reply on the part of the government, in order to reassure Canadians who are asking themselves a lot of serious questions in this regard.
I do not wish to take any more of the time of the house; the main purpose of my intervention being a specific reply. I trust the reply of the government will be as favourable.

maintopic: CONSUMER AFFAIRS-REQUEST THAT PROTECTION BE INCLUDED IN CRIMINAL CODE
CONSUMER AFFAIRS-REQUEST THAT PROTECTION BE INCLUDED IN CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago I asked the Minister of Justice the following question:
In view of the fact that the housewives' charter to protect the consumer has now become part of Britain's criminal code, will the minister introduce similar legislation or consider such action in connection with his new omnibus bill to amend the Canadian Criminal Code?
The minister replied that he would certainly want to talk that over with the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. I hope he has done so.
The speeches of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs are studded with declarations that the consumer has the right to be protected from fraud, deception, misleading advertising and other unscrupulous malpractices. Surely the time has come to legislate firmly, clearly and unmistakably against this sort of thing. We need teeth in the Criminal Code to protect the consumer. If the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is to live up to the first half of his title, that is, if he is to be the watchdog for the consumer, he will have to be given the necessary legal teeth.
In Britain they have taken a long step forward in the direction of protecting the consumer from fraud. The housewives' charter, which became part of Britain's criminal code last month, deals with business ethics. A board of trade spokesman describes it as a law vitally important to the whole community. It is designed to give safeguards to everyone who buys goods and services. It requires
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion merchants, when describing their goods, to tell it as it is. Details such as size, manufacture and performance must be given correctly. The same thing applies to certain statements describing services.
For the first time the law extends not only to written but also to oral descriptions. The law requires local weights and measures authorities to enforce it. The housewives' charter, technically known as the trade descriptions act, 1968, has been in the making for several years. At the time of its introduction into the British parliament in the spring of 1966 one British newspaper commented:
Publicity about the penalties may have the deterrent effect which is needed, without the prospect opening up of butchers or bakers or candlestick makers, being prosecuted by the dozen.
The strict provisions of the new law are clearly designed to curb the malpractices of a few businessmen and their employees in the hope that this protection for the consumer will build up his and her trust in the marketplace.
If we had such legislation in Canada there would be means of inquiring into and dealing with advertising which is mailed wholesale to customers, such as that which I drew to the attention of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs recently. It begins:
You have already won a great art treasure! Congratulations! You have already won ... an oil painting by Renoir! or an etching by Rembrandt! or a woodcut by Holbein! or a lithograph by Chagall! or a silk-screen by Warhol! or a lithograph by Picasso! or, at the very least, you have certainly won a full colour reproduction of a Gainsborough!
All of which, and much more, is designed to sell an encyclopaedia. What is sold in the process is an unprotected public.
This type of promotion demands the closest scrutiny by public authorities. It is misleading for the very reason that it is so well written. Thousands of Canadians are led to believe that they are already well on their way to possessing a priceless art treasure. Only the fine print indicates that this so-called contest is open to residents of the United States as well, that it is void where prohibited by federal, state, provincial or local laws or regulations, and that there is only one prize per family.
The letter authenticating the top prize-the Renoir-was sent by an American appraiser to an American publishing firm over 18 months ago. Who is to say that this contest was not available to residents of the United States much earlier than to residents of Canada? Who is to say that any Canadian has a
December 12, 1968

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion chance for more than the booby prize-the coloured reproduction of the Gainsborough, costing a few cents? This whole matter bristles with questions demanding answers that can be given only after proper investigation. The public has a right to be protected from misleading advertising.
The fact that this particular advertising emanated from Maclean's in Toronto led me to believe that the publishers of that well known magazine were responsible, although the two addresses were different. Further investigation indicates that the two Maclean's inhabit a single building on the corner of University and Dundas streets in Toronto, hence the two addresses. It would appear that this is one of those perfect marriages where the two have become a single whole. In any event, the evidence available leads one to that conclusion.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
All of this, Mr. Speaker, points up the need in Canada for legislation to protect the consumer from misleading advertising and other malpractices of the marketplace. I urge upon the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) or for that matter the Minister of Corporate and Consumer Affairs (Mr. Basford), the need for a housewives' charter as part of Canada's Criminal Code.

I do not want to disappoint the hon. lady, but my officials have examined it and have advised me that most of the provisions of the shoppers' charter in Britain are already contained in the laws of Canada, principally in section 33(c) of the Combines Investigation Act and section 306 of the Criminal Code. As the hon. lady knows, the latter is to be transferred from the Criminal Code to the Combines Investigation Act so that I can have direct administrative responsibility for it. If we were to pass the motion now before the house, dealing with procedural reform, we could undoubtedly get to that more quickly than we will be able to do now. There is protection also in many of the provincial consumer protection acts, as well as the sale of goods acts. The point I am making is that much of what the British have done, we have already done in Canada or have under active consideration.

We have already examined the British charter. I have a special assistant on my staff in charge of consumer affairs who will be spending three days in London in the early part of January examining this and other consumer programs in Britain, and judging their suitability to Canadian conditions. I should like also to make the point to the hon. member that at the first meeting of the consumer council which I appointed in November and which met on Monday, I said to the council:
It seems to me that it would be useful to have before the public, before industry, before consumer groups, and before government, a declaration of consumer rights, and I would hope your council would endeavour to draw up such a declaration. Such a declaration should attempt to set out those consumer rights that will ensure that the consumer benefits from our competitive economic system. It could serve as a guide for the conduct of further debate on consumer affairs... It would clarify for all sectors of our economy precisely what the consumer demands of his economy and his society.
So, I think in asking the consumer council to prepare a declaration or charter of consumer rights, undoubtedly I have been a step ahead of what the hon. lady is urging. maintopic: UNIDENTIFIED FLYING OBJECTS-REPORTED SIGHTINGS OVER SIOUX LOOKOUT, ONTARIO
UNIDENTIFIED FLYING OBJECTS-REPORTED SIGHTINGS OVER SIOUX LOOKOUT, ONTARIO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 4,	1968, I
addressed a question to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux) concerning
December 12, 1968

the alleged sighting of unidentified flying objects over the town of Sioux Lookout, Ontario. I did this deliberately because the Department of National Defence maintains a very thorough, and I would probably say expensive, radar detection establishment at Sioux Lookout. I also thought this would be an opportunity for the Department of National Defence to shed some light on this phenomenon of unidentified flying objects.
If I were a pilot of one of these U.F.O.'s I am certain that I could think of no better place to land and examine planet Earth than Sioux Lookout, Ontario, the people of which have a tremendous capacity for offering hospitality that is exceeded only by their ability to out-enjoy visitors.
In a more serious vein, there have been a number of sightings located in the general area of northwestern Ontario. Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, you will recall an instance where the hon. member for Selkirk brought to the attention of the house the rather spectacular experiences of people in the Falcon lake area. However, no satisfaction was ever given the hon. member, and if the government has any information at all about these matters I think it should be made available to the public. There is, as hon. members know, a great deal of curiosity about this subject.
Shortly after my last visit to Sioux Lookout I was told by telephone, and in person, that there had been a large number of sightings there. An article appeared in the town's paper, the Daily Bulletin, which I should like to quote to bear out my claim that there have been extensive sightings in this area. This is the November 29 edition of the paper, and the article reads as follows:
For the last two evenings several people in town have sighted an unidentified flying object over Pelican lake.
Last night's sighting was observed by quite a few people outside Jim's Coffee Bar on Front street at about 6.00 p.m. The only information we could gather from observers was that it "was a big light in the sky, which kept changing in colour". No idea as to its shape or manoeuvreability was given. About a month ago, at least five people saw an U.F.O. Four on a return trip from Dryden spotted a green light in the sky near the "Turkey Trail" while another person in town saw the same phenomenon about two hours earlier over Pelican lake.
Both descriptions tallied on checking them out and the U.F.O. was described as a flat circular object of bright greenish hue, which appeared to be pulsating. It was travelling at conventional
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
speed for an airborne object and glided down behind the tree line out of sight.
Then the article concludes with the question: Anyone have an explanation?
That brings me to the point of my question, Mr. Speaker. We do have this very extensive facility at Sioux Lookout that is operated by the Department of National Defence. Surely if anything was in the sky over that period, records would be kept by this most efficient establishement, one which, I might add, is also an expensive establishment. Therefore I should like to ask the parliamentary secretary-and it is very kind of him to stay up so late-whether he could release some of this supposedly confidential information for the benefit of the Canadian public. The Christmas holiday season is fast approaching, but I do not want to receive the answer from the parliamentary secretary that it was Santa Claus trying out his reindeer in anticipation of Christmas.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. W. Groos (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
maintopic: UNIDENTIFIED FLYING OBJECTS-REPORTED SIGHTINGS OVER SIOUX LOOKOUT, ONTARIO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope I am not setting a precedent this evening by answering this question, but questions relating to unidentified flying objects should really be directed to the minister who speaks on behalf of the National Research Council. However I undertook to check out the observations made by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, and I am informed that although there were some strange lights noticed in the Sioux Lookout area on the night of November 27, no radar reflections were picked up by the radar station at Sioux Lookout.
I do not like to disappoint the hon. member, but may I take this opportunity to forecast to him that there probably will be some unidentified flying objects picked up by that radar station on the night of December 24. There is some evidence that these will eventually be identified as a space vehicle propelled by eight unknown objects, and this will be reported through the regular NORAD channels. It is highly unlikely, however, that the pilot of this space vehicle on that night will be identified either as the hon. member for Hamilton West or the hon. member for Edmonton Centre.
